rows.de_laurence: No footnote, and no footnote marker after 'homage.'
rows.crowley: Footnote 1 on 'homage': 'I am not responsible for this ultra-Arian confusion of persons.—ED.'
rows.note: Crowley's own editorial note (signed ED.) is in the 1904 print (scan printed p. 13). De Laurence dropped it. His page image (p035_a) shows no marker and no note. This is the only change to Bael.

rows.de_laurence: (8.) VASSAGO
rows.crowley: (3.) VASSAGO
rows.note: This is a misprint in de Laurence (page image p035_b, his printed p. 22). The running text still says 'The Third Spirit', and the 1904 print (p. 13) correctly reads (3.).

rows.de_laurence: sitting upon a Pale-Coloured Horse.
rows.crowley: sitting upon a pale-coloured [Horse?].
rows.note: This is a real edition difference. The 1904 print (OCR of djvu p.31: 'Pale-coloured [Horse ?]') marks 'Horse' as a conjecture with brackets and a query. De Laurence drops the brackets and the query and prints 'Horse' as plain text, so the reading looks certain.

rows.de_laurence: (no footnote; de Laurence p.27 has no note, and the text runs straight on to Sallos)
rows.crowley: Mathers (TRANS.): the word is left out in some older codices and indistinct in others but appears to be 'horse', so it is bracketed. Crowley (ED.): 'The Quartos have "ass"'.
rows.note: De Laurence leaves out both the translator's note and Crowley's editorial note. So the reader loses the textual doubt and the alternative reading 'ass' from the Quartos.

rows.de_laurence: His appearance is comely
rows.crowley: His appearing is comely
rows.note: A real difference, checked on both page images: de Laurence p. 28 (p041_a) and the 1904 scan p. 17 (djvu page 31). De Laurence changed 'appearing' to 'appearance'. The meaning is the same. This is the only verbal change de Laurence made to the text of spirits 19-27.

rows.de_laurence: (sentence absent) ... He speaketh with a very clear and subtle Voice. He governeth 26 Legions of Spirits.
rows.crowley: He speaketh with a very clear and subtle Voice. He is a Great Liar and not to be trusted unto. He governeth 26 Legions of Spirits.
rows.note: This is a real difference between the editions. I checked the scan of the 1904 print (Wikimedia djvu page 33, printed p. 19), and it reads 'He is a Great Liar, and not to be trusted unto.' So de Laurence cut the sentence; Celephaïs did not add it. Without it, de Laurence's Berith is a truthful spirit, while the 1904 Berith is a liar who gives true answers.

rows.de_laurence: No note on 'true answers, Past, Present, and to Come'. The page's notes are 1 Figure 30, 2 Figure 31, 3 See ante, Spirit No. 13.
rows.crowley: Mathers' note on 'to Come': 'This hardly agrees with the statement that he is a great liar, and not to be trusted.'
rows.note: De Laurence removed the note together with the sentence it comments on, and renumbered the remaining notes. The 1904 print numbers them 1 Figure 30, 2 Figure 31, 3 'This hardly agrees...', 4 See ante (checked on the scan).

rows.de_laurence: Then he will speak marvellously of all wonderful Sciences
rows.crowley: Then will he speak marvellously of all wonderful Sciences
rows.note: Only the word order changes; the meaning is the same. I checked de Laurence against his page image (printed p. 34) and the 1904 reading against an OCR of the 1904 scan (djvu p. 36, printed p. 22). The Celephaïs 2003 re-set has de Laurence's order here, not the 1904 order. The other differences ('great' vs 'Great', 'Thirty-Seventh' vs 'Thirty-seventh') are capitalisation only and are ignored.

rows.de_laurence: Halphas, or Malthous (or Malthas) (the heading still reads HALPHAS, or MALTHUS)
rows.crowley: Halphas, or Malthus (or Malthas) (heading and body agree)
rows.note: I confirmed 'Malthous' on de Laurence's page image (printed p. 34, p047_b), so it is not a transcriber slip. The 1904 scan (OCR of djvu p. 36) and the Celephaïs re-set both read 'Malthus'. In de Laurence the heading says Malthus and the body says Malthous, so his book disagrees with itself.

rows.de_laurence: Only Mathers's note: 'Or Warriors, or Men-at-Arms.'
rows.crowley: Mathers's note plus Crowley's note ² signed ED.: 'But Malthus is certainly in heaven. See "Prometheus Unbound," Introduction by P. B. Shelley ...'
rows.note: de Laurence leaves out Crowley's joke footnote about Malthus. The 1904 scan OCR confirms the note is on printed p. 22. This fits the rest of the book, where de Laurence cuts Crowley's ED. material.

rows.de_laurence: No footnote on the legion count ('He governeth 30 Legions').
rows.crowley: Footnote ¹ on '30': 'Three is given instead of 30 in several Codices; but 30 is probably the more correct.'
rows.note: de Laurence drops Mathers's note on the variant legion count; the page image (printed p. 35, p048_b) has no footnote marker and no note. The number in the text, 30, is the same in both. The OCR of the 1904 scan (djvu p. 37, printed p. 23) confirms the note is in the 1904 edition.

rows.de_laurence: No footnote after 'thereon.'
rows.crowley: Footnote ² after 'thereon.': 'In several Codices this passage reads: "His Office is to Guide the Waters and Ships laden with Armour thereon."'
rows.note: de Laurence drops Mathers's note giving the shorter reading from other codices; his page image (printed p. 35, p048_b) has no marker. The OCR of the 1904 scan (djvu p. 37, printed p. 23) confirms the note is in the 1904 edition. The missing comma in 'Strong and appeareth' is punctuation only.

rows.de_laurence: Two seals: printed figures 47 and 48. The second has a different drawing, with three crosses on top.
rows.crowley: The seals are not in the Crowley transcription, which says the seal images are printed on separate plates and were not included.
rows.note: de Laurence gives Vepar two seals. This is the only spirit from 37 to 45 with more than one, and it shifts his figure numbering by one from here on. I could not check whether the 1904 plates also show two Vepar seals, so this is not confirmed as a difference between the editions.

rows.de_laurence: Heading: (44.) SHAN.
rows.crowley: Heading: (44.) SHAX.
rows.note: A misprint in de Laurence's heading. I confirmed it on his page image (printed p. 36, p049_a/b), so it is not a transcriber slip. The body of his entry reads 'Shax, or Shaz (or Shass)' as in the 1904 edition, and the rim of his seal reads S H A X. The OCR of the 1904 scan (djvu p. 38, printed p. 24) confirms the heading SHAX.

rows.de_laurence: '6 Legions' has no footnote. Checked on the page image (printed p. 37): there is no marker after 6, and the only footnote on the page is the Coptic note to spirit 47.
rows.crowley: '6² Legions', with footnote ² 'Should probably be 60 instead of 6.' (unsigned, so it is the translator's note)
rows.note: Both print the figure 6, but de Laurence drops the 1904 note doubting it. A reader of de Laurence alone would not know the 1904 edition suggests 60.

rows.de_laurence: to procure the Love of Woman
rows.crowley: to procure the Love of Women
rows.note: The page image (printed p. 37) confirms 'Woman' is in de Laurence's print, so it is not a transcription slip. Singular instead of plural: a small change of sense, from women in general to a woman.

rows.de_laurence: The Forty-seventh Spirit Uvall, or Vual, or Voval.
rows.crowley: The Forty-seventh Spirit is Uvall, or Vual, or Voval.
rows.note: De Laurence drops the verb 'is'; the page image confirms it. This is a typesetting slip and does not change the meaning.

rows.de_laurence: carrieth a Boshawk upon his Fist
rows.crowley: carrieth a Goshawk upon his Fist
rows.note: The page image (printed p. 39) confirms that de Laurence's print really reads 'Boshawk'. It is a misprint in the 1916 book, not an error by our transcriber. 'Boshawk' is not a word, so the bird is lost in de Laurence.

rows.de_laurence: CAIM / Caim (no diaeresis, in the heading and the text)
rows.crowley: CAÏM / Caïm (with diaeresis)
rows.note: The page image (printed p. 39) confirms there is no diaeresis in de Laurence. It only changes the spelling (the diaeresis marks Ca-ïm as two syllables); the name is the same.

rows.de_laurence: He governeth 30¹ Legions of Spirits
rows.crowley: He governeth 3¹ Legions of Spirits
rows.note: This is a real change, confirmed on the de Laurence page image (p. 41, p054_a, where the printed figure is clearly "30" with the note marker). The 1904 text gives 3 Legions and adds a note suggesting 30. De Laurence silently changed the number in the text to 30 but kept the note marker, so his note now "corrects" a number that is already correct.

rows.de_laurence: ¹ Should be 30. For these 72 Great Spirits of the Book Goetia are all Princes and Leaders of numbers.
rows.crowley: ¹ Should probably be 30. For these 72 Great Spirits of the Book Goetia are all Princes and Leaders of numbers.
rows.note: De Laurence drops "probably", turning the 1904 editor's tentative suggestion into a firm statement, which fits his change to the text itself (confirmed on image p054_b).

rows.de_laurence: Handcrafts
rows.crowley: Handicrafts
rows.note: Confirmed in the de Laurence print (p. 41, image p054_b: "Handcrafts"), so it is not a transcription slip. It is only a spelling variant and the meaning does not change.

rows.de_laurence: governeth 50 Legions of Spirits
rows.crowley: governeth 80¹ Legions of Spirits
rows.note: This is the only real textual change in 64-72. De Laurence prints 50 in the body text, which is the number from Crowley's editorial note ('The actual number is 50'), and drops the 1904 reading of 80. Checked on the page image (printed p. 44): it clearly reads 50 and has no footnote marker. The Celephaïs re-set also reads 80 with the 'Perhaps an error for 30' note, so the 1904 reading is confirmed twice.

rows.de_laurence: (no footnote)
rows.crowley: Perhaps an error for 30.—TRANS. The actual number is 50; at least it was in 1898.—ED.
rows.note: De Laurence leaves out both Mathers' note suggesting 30 and Crowley's note giving 50 'as of 1898'. He writes Crowley's figure into the text without saying where it came from, so readers of the 1916 edition lose the fact that the manuscript number was 80.

rows.de_laurence: a Star in a Pentacle, at first
rows.crowley: a Star in a Pentacle, ⛤, at first
rows.note: De Laurence leaves out the printed pentagram sign that the 1904 text puts after 'Pentacle' (checked on the page image, printed p. 44). He keeps the matching triangle sign in Haures (64). The meaning does not change, but the 1904 sign shows that the 'Pentacle' here is a five-pointed star.

rows.de_laurence: to declare the Secret Counsel of any one
rows.crowley: to declare the Secret Counsels of any one
rows.note: Singular against plural. De Laurence's 'Counsel' is confirmed on the page image (printed p. 45). The 1904 hand transcription and the Celephaïs re-set both read 'Counsels'. The change in meaning is very small: a person's secret counsel in general, rather than their individual secrets.
